E0376.summary: For Atwood, the longing of the mind for its object, through which the research is ultimately made manifest and which prayer enlarges.
E0376.body: Atwood speaks of the inquiry as “a research which is so much wrapped in and about the Desire as to be ultimately made manifest through its means” [III.4 ¶20]. She treats every desire as a kind of prayer, and prayer in turn works “(by enlarging the desire)” [III.4 ¶24]. The record suggests Desire is the motive force of the method: the research depends on it and comes to light through it.

E0377.summary: Scriptural book Atwood cites in support of the unfigured form of the Divine Essence.
E0377.body: Atwood cites Deuteronomy 4:15, “Take good heed unto yourselves, for ye saw no manner of similitude on the say that the Lord spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire” [II.3 ¶48; II.3 n52], to support her point that the Divine Essence is without figure.

E0378.summary: In Eudoxus, what the wise make fall upon the earth so that it yields precious fruit; not further explained.
E0378.body: Spoken by Eudoxus (quoted): the wise make it fall upon the earth, “knowing how to make the dew of Heaven fall upon it” [IV.3 ¶12], so that it bears precious fruit. The text does not explain the expression further; its plain meaning in the method is unclear.

E0379.summary: In Rabbi Ben Jocahi, the dew shaken from the head of the hidden principle, which awakens the dead and nourishes the saints; identified with manna.
E0379.body: Quoted from Rabbi Ben Jocahi: “Thy dew is the dew of light” [III.2 ¶3]. This dew falls from the head of the hidden principle, awakens the dead, nourishes the saints and is white as the diamond. It is identified with manna: “It is this which nourishes the most exalted saints, the manna which descends into the field of sacred fruits” [III.2 ¶3].

E0380.summary: For Atwood, a figure of the First Matter and refulgent Light: the wholeness of the Fundamental Nature personified, containing all elements of being.
E0380.body: Atwood presents Diana as the First Matter and the refulgent Light, personifying the whole Fundamental Nature, inferior and superior together: “she is the wholeness of the Fundamental Nature at once personified, the knot and link of all the elements o being” [III.1 ¶70].

E0381.summary: A term in a Proclus passage, named alongside 'our individual reason'; not further defined.
E0381.body: Appears in a passage of Proclus (quoted), where the spirit “becomes perfectly everything from which dianoia and our individual reason consist” [II.2 ¶15]. The text gives no further definition; it is apparently a reasoning faculty listed beside individual reason.

E0382.summary: Author of de Quintessentia, cited by Atwood for an account of powder of transmutation found in Lully's Westminster cell.
E0382.body: Atwood cites E. Dickenson's *de Quintessentia* for the story of powder of transmutation discovered in Lully's cell at Westminster [I.1 ¶47; I.1 n57]. She uses it as reported testimony; the records show no comment from her on it.

E0383.summary: John Digby, given as translator of the French edition of Sendivogius' New Light of Alchemy (London 1722), which adds the Treatise on Salt and a Dialogue.
E0383.body: Named in a note on Sendivogius' *New Light of Alchemy*, London 1722: Digby translated from the French edition, which adds the Treatise on Salt and an instructive Dialogue [I.1 ¶71; I.1 n91]. Atwood refers to this as Digby's edition.

E0384.summary: An operation by which the powder is multiplied, and a measured process required before perfect dissolution and before extraction of the Fixed Salt.
E0384.body: Two quoted voices use the term. An adept (quoted) says the white or red powder is multiplied tenfold with each digestion, and “each digestion is made in tenfold shorter time than the preceding” [II.1 ¶25]. Eudoxus (quoted) requires digestion before perfect dissolution in the Second Key, “after a proportioned digestion and putrefaction” [IV.3 ¶5], and before extracting the Fixed Salt in the Third Key, by “a convenient digestion and a slow distillation” [IV.3 ¶7]. In both cases it is a measured, staged operation within the work.

E0385.summary: Authority cited by Atwood for the divine darkness, visible yet incomprehensible, and for the True Thing of negative theology.
E0385.body: Atwood cites Dionysius in support of the divine darkness, the “caligo divina” [III.2 ¶13], which is visible yet beyond comprehension. She also draws on him for the True Thing of negative theology, whose possession is the happiest life [III.2 ¶15]. She uses him with approval.

E0386.summary: Plato's correspondent; Atwood thinks a practical science drew him to Plato.
E0386.body: Named as Plato's correspondent. Atwood suggests he was drawn to Plato by a science she believes was practical [I.1 ¶17].

E0387.summary: Speaker in the Banquet, cited by Atwood in support of the idea that the wise mind possesses its object within itself.
E0387.body: Atwood cites Diotima in the *Banquet* in support of the idea that a wise mind holds its object within itself: “that mind which is become wise needs not to investigate any further” [II.1 ¶37]. She uses the passage with approval.

E0388.summary: Critics of Alchemy whose 'learned cavils and clamours' Atwood dismisses.
E0388.body: Atwood criticizes the disappointed chemists for their learned cavils and clamours against Alchemy [IV.4 ¶12]. She rejects their view.

E0389.summary: Anonymous voice, endorsed by Atwood, who treats material gifts as tokens of the Spirit's love.
E0389.body: A quoted disciple says of the Spirit: “then he sends us these things as tokens and pledges of his love” [IV.3 ¶46]. Atwood endorses this reading of material gifts as signs of the Spirit's love.

E0390.summary: In Proclus, meeting, union with and direct sight of the Father; not opinion or science but Intellectual Vision; the Paternal Port.
E0390.body: Defined by Proclus (quoted): “For discovery is this, --- to meet with him, to be united to Him, and to see Him Himself” [II.4 ¶41]. It is not opinion and not science but Intellectual Vision of the Father or Maker. Proclus equates it with the Paternal Port: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father” [II.4 ¶41].

E0391.summary: In Plotinus, the ordinary reasoning into which the soul falls back from Intellect after the divine state.
E0391.body: Plotinus (quoted) describes the soul after the divine state as “falling off from Intellect into the discursive energy of reason” [III.2 ¶50]. It names ordinary step-by-step reasoning, a lower condition than Intellect.

E0392.summary: The reasoning faculty which, Atwood says, plays no part in discovering and assenting to universal propositions.
E0392.body: Atwood says that in discovering universal propositions and assenting to them “there is no use of the discursive faculty or of external facts to witness” [II.1 ¶34]. Knowledge of this kind does not come by reasoning or from outside evidence.

E0393.summary: For Atwood, the core operation of the first work: an artificial loosening of the vital bond that dissolves the fixed sensual compact so the spirit can be renovated and perfected.
E0393.body:
Atwood treats dissolution as the central operation of the first work. “The beginning of the whole work is a perfect solution” [IV.1 ¶4]: the subject is dissolved in its own blood, or own mercury, to remove superfluities. The dissolution must be total, for “nothing short of dissolution can give it rest” [IV.1 ¶7].

She takes the term from the old doctrine: “We adopt the term dissolve here in accordance with the old doctrine” [II.3 n2]. She applies it to the change in the vital relation during trance, and notes that the Alchemists say the sensible medium ought to be dissolved. She calls it “an artificial dissolution of the vital bond, by means of Alchemy” [I.3 n64]. The philosophic work begins after it, and by it vapour, blackness and death are driven out: “and this by dissolution” [I.3 ¶56].

In the process, “that which was fixed, viz., the sensual compact, is dissolved, and that which is dissolved is renovated”, and “by Dissolution thou shalt possess a triumphant reward” [II.3 ¶37]. The process is repeated: “the process by which the spirit is carried on from each succeeding dissolution into a more perfect form of being” [I.3 n19]. In the same note Atwood says a radical dissolution of the spirit reveals the evil of original sin, and that dissolution by the water is the key of restoration [I.3 n19].

She also describes it as the breaking-up of the light's body and of the natural-born life, in which the three principles separate: “an eclipsation of the light takes place, and a dissolution of its body” [III.1 ¶53]. The context suggests its cause is vital heat artificially stirred in the blood [III.1 ¶53].

E0394.summary: For Atwood, the divided condition reached by 'falling off', in which one ceases to be the Universe.
E0394.body: Atwood writes that by falling off, “in becoming dividual, he ceases to be the Universe” [IV.4 ¶27]. It names the separated state opposed to unity with the whole.

E0395.summary: Atwood's name for the Art in its higher purposes: working in and with the Universal Spirit, joined with universal theosophy, beyond its mineral uses.
E0395.body:
Atwood uses Divine Art as a name for the Art. Boehme gives the “principles of the Divine Art” and a ground of experience for it [I.1 ¶68]. She separates its mineral uses (quickening and perfecting) from “the higher purposes and application of the Divine Art, and universal theosophy” [I.1 ¶42]. It requires a representative of the rebellious Principle: “that identical representative of him which the Divine Art requires” [III.1 ¶64]. Nearby text speaks of “the Hermetic Art”, but the records do not say the two names are identical [III.1 ¶66].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “the Divine Art works in and with the Universal Spirit” [APP ¶140]. There it brings forth various states of life that offer allurements to the will, and it uses instruments as well as vessels [APP ¶140].

E0396.summary: For Atwood, the loosening of the bond between spirit and its bodily media, which Paracelsus speaks of and mesmerism imitates externally.
E0396.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls mesmeric practice “an imitation of the Divine Art of the separation of which Paracelsus speaks” [APP ¶73]. The Art apparently loosens the bond between spirit and its bodily media; mesmerism imitates it only outwardly.

E0397.summary: For Atwood, a state in which, while it lasts, subject and object are not two in consciousness.
E0397.body: Atwood writes that “as in the Divine conjunction, whilst it lasts, there are not two things as of subject and object in the consciousness” [III.2 ¶66]. In it, the life that understands and the light understood are one.

E0398.summary: For Atwood, an ecstasy kindled in connection with its Source, which draws nature to its desire and works the whole miracle of the Hermetic Art.
E0398.body: Atwood speaks of “that kindling of Divine Ecstasy, in connection with its Source” [III.1 ¶70]. It draws nature to its desire and works the whole miracle of the Hermetic Art. It is apparently the active power that accomplishes the work.

E0399.summary: For Atwood, that with which the resigned Spirit is clothed; it qualifies the true Adept and is identified with the material of the Corner-Stone.
E0399.body: Atwood says the resigned Spirit is clothed with the Divine Essentiality: “And this Essentiality it is which qualifies the true Adept” [III.3 ¶24]. It also sanctifies the Adept. She identifies it with the material of the Corner-Stone: “It is this material of the Corner-Stone which links reason to Divinity” [III.3 ¶24].

E0400.summary: The first and most beautiful objects of Wisdom: undecaying and invariable, with other things beautiful by participating in them.
E0400.body: The phrase is Atwood's gloss on Iamblicus (quoted): Wisdom is “conversant with the first and most beautiful objects (i.e., the Divine Exemplars)” [II.1 ¶39]. They do not decay or vary, and other things are beautiful by participating in them.

E0401.summary: Addressed by Atwood as the august Mother of all things; at the Substant Unity, Experience is present with Power.
E0401.body: Atwood addresses it directly: “And thou august Mother of all things, Divine Experience.” [III.3 ¶79]. She describes the Substant Unity as the place “where Experience is present with Power, and Effect in substance to bear them witness” [III.3 ¶79].

E0402.summary: For Atwood, the inner faculty of perception which, purified and strengthened, perceives the truth of all beings.
E0402.body: Atwood, citing Plato, speaks of “that divine eye which, as Plato says, is better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes” [II.2 ¶8]. Purified and strengthened, this inner faculty perceives the truth of all beings.

E0403.summary: For Atwood, the divine command that blesses the union of Soul and Passive Spirit, in which the sensual dominant is occultated and subdued.
E0403.body: Atwood writes that “the Divine Fiat comes mercifully to bless the union” of Soul and Passive Spirit [III.3 ¶10]. In it the sensual dominant is subdued: “when the sensual dominant is occultated in the Divine Fiat and subdued” [III.3 ¶15].

E0404.summary: In Iamblicus, what is received in perfect plenitude through the third class of prayer, the final seal of union.
E0404.body: Iamblicus (quoted) writes that “through the energy of the third, we receive a perfect plenitude of Divine Fire” [III.4 ¶24]. The third class of prayer is the final seal of union.

E0405.summary: For Atwood, the divine seed in man, beheld in a deformed condition under the evils of its birth.
E0405.body: Atwood refers to “the divine germ of humanity said to be beheld under the thousand evils of its birth” [II.3 ¶30]. In that state it appears deformed.
